note: Heart rate is context, not a diagnosis. Healthy-volunteer demo; no clinical effect is claimed. Sources verified against the originals on 2026-10-24 unless marked secondary.

bernardi2006.design: 24 healthy adults (12 musicians); 6 tracks at 55-150 bpm in random order; a random 2-min silent pause
findings: Faster tempo raised heart rate, blood pressure and breathing.
The slowest track (raga, 55 bpm) gave a significantly larger fall in heart rate (p < 0.01).
The silent pause lowered heart rate, blood pressure and ventilation even below baseline.
Effects depended on tempo rather than style; preference did not explain them.
bernardi2006.caveat: Small, healthy, young volunteers; 2-4 min exposures.

bradt2013.cite: Bradt, Dileo & Potvin (2013), Cochrane Review CD006577: music for stress and anxiety in coronary heart disease
findings: Heart rate: mean difference -3.40 bpm (95% CI -6.12 to -0.69).
Anxiety reduction was greatest when patients chose the music (SMD -0.89).
bradt2013.caveat: Small trials, many at high risk of bias; 'quality of the evidence is not strong'.

zhang2026.cite: Zhang et al. (2026), Frontiers in Psychology: music intervention and HRV, meta-analysis of 24 RCTs
findings: Short interventions (<= 30 min) were particularly effective for HFnu.
Participant-selected music yielded superior outcomes to standardized music.
zhang2026.caveat: HRV outcomes (we use HR only); subgroup findings from few studies; high heterogeneity.

kim2018.cite: Kim et al. (2018), Psychiatry Investigation: stress and HRV review
findings: Heart rate tends to rise under stress.
HR is also affected by posture, activity, caffeine, smoking, age and medications such as beta-blockers; pair with self-report.
kim2018.caveat: Narrative review; no standard definition of stress.

vieira_mri.cite: Vieira et al., Radiography: music interventions during MRI (via news summary)
findings: Lower heart rate with music; some fast or aggressive patient picks did not help.
vieira_mri.caveat: Secondary source; the primary paper was not checked.

rules.text: If the patient says stop, go silent and stay silent until they re-enable audio.
Fade out and pause while a nurse or clinician is present.
Only play tracks the patient approved from the calm list.
Calm list = steady tempo of roughly 55-70 bpm. The slowest tempo gave the largest heart-rate fall.
Exclude fast or high-energy tracks (around 100 bpm and up raised heart rate).
Silence is a real option: if heart rate stays elevated during music, try a silent pause.
Keep music sessions to about 30 minutes, then pause and re-evaluate.
Expect a few bpm at most; judge by the trend back toward baseline, not by a target number.
A heart-rate rise is a physiological change, not anxiety. Ignore rises caused by movement.
Tie-breaker: prefer fewer note onsets, lower loudness, steadier dynamics and less treble. Not tested in the trials above.
Tie-breaker: prefer tracks whose HKU956 listeners' heart rate drifted down. Observational only (self-chosen songs, ~50 s plays), not causal.
